paras: The attempted lynching of Fred Jackson took place at Oxford, Connecticut, on the night of February 25, 1903, when woodchoppers beat Jackson, a Black man, in a hotel barroom and hunted him through the woods threatening to lynch him. Jackson had just been released by the coroner, who found insufficient evidence that he had killed a French Canadian woodchopper, Henry Resnet. He escaped, and the New-York Tribune reported the coroner's finding under the headline "Mob's Verdict Not Sustained."

Resnet's burned body was found in the ruins of his hut on land owned by John B. Pope in Oxford early on February 24. Coroner Mix of New Haven and Medical Examiner Barnes were said to have found a deep gash in the body, and an odor of kerosene was reported at the ruins. Jackson, who said he had slept in the hut that night, was arrested and held at the Seymour lockup, and a knife found on him was taken for examination.

The two men had shared the hut until a recent quarrel, but Jackson had told Pope the day before that they had patched up their differences. In a statement on February 25, Jackson said he woke to find the hut full of smoke, blamed a spark from the drunken Resnet's pipe, and said the stain on his knife came from opening a can of tomatoes. Constable Hubbell, the first to reach the fire, said he saw nothing of Jackson there.

Coroner Mix released Jackson on the evening of February 25, and Jackson went straight back to Oxford, where friends of the dead man had gathered in the barroom of the Oxford hotel. According to a New Haven dispatch, he was refused a drink and two woodchoppers beat him badly; the wire account described a quarrel with several woodchoppers in which he was "pummeled severely." The bartender got him out of the room and told him to make for the woods, and the Tribune's correspondent wrote that only the bartender's ruse saved his life.

Angered, the woodchoppers threatened the bartender and searched the premises before learning that Jackson had fled. A gang of them, mostly French Canadians and numbering about a dozen by the Tribune's count, spent the night searching the woods between Oxford and Derby, threatening to kill him if they found him. By the next morning the search had failed, and it was thought that Jackson would get away.

On February 27 Coroner Mix said his finding would be that Resnet was murdered but that the evidence did not warrant holding Jackson, and the report was filed that day. The excitement among the woodchoppers was then reported to have abated, and Jackson had not been seen since he took to the woods. No report of an arrest of any of the woodchoppers, or of Jackson's later whereabouts, appears in the coverage.

Connecticut dispatches in the Waterbury Democrat and the New Haven Journal and Courier first reported the case, and the wire carried it to Rhode Island and Maine. Before the mob action, the Portland Daily Press headlined the arrest "Death of Negro in Connecticut." The Oxford wire on the hunt ran as "Threaten to Lynch Negro" in the Providence News, as "Hunting for Jackson" in the Waterbury Democrat, and as "Swear Vengeance" in the Daily Kennebec Journal, reporting the threats without comment.

The New-York Tribune's Derby correspondent relayed the woodchoppers' case against Jackson as their assertion and wrote that "all Oxford" was angry over his release. Its follow-up the next day presented the coroner's report as a rejection of the "angry mob" and its verdict. Le Messager, a French-language paper in Lewiston, Maine, printed the wire under "Ils veulent lyncher un nègre," placing Oxford in New Brunswick. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

Accounts of Resnet's death conflicted: the Tribune reported the woodchoppers' claim that Jackson was met coming from the burning cabin, while Constable Hubbell said he saw nothing of Jackson at the fire. A New Haven dispatch of February 26 expected the coroner to find the death accidental, but the coroner's own later statement called it murder while clearing Jackson for lack of evidence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Fred Jackson
bases: After a coroner released Fred Jackson, a Black man suspected in a woodchopper's death, a gang of woodchoppers beat him and hunted him through the woods threatening to lynch or kill him (A6, A11, A13).

Jackson was beaten and pursued by a gang the Tribune put at 'a dozen' woodchoppers acting on their belief that he had murdered Resnet after the coroner freed him (A6, A11), but no paper reports that he was killed; it was an attempted lynching (A13).

The Oxford wire (A6, A7), a separate New Haven dispatch (A8) and the Tribune's own Derby telegraph (A11) independently report the beating and the hunt, and the Tribune follow-up confirms the mob's pursuit (A13).

framing.detail: The Oxford wire ran as 'Threaten to Lynch Negro' (Providence), 'Hunting for Jackson' with the deck 'if the Negro Is Found He Will Roughly Handled' (Waterbury) and 'Swear Vengeance' (Augusta), reporting the threats without comment.
The New-York Tribune's first story relayed the woodchoppers' case against Jackson as their assertions, then headed its follow-up 'Mob's Verdict Not Sustained' after the coroner cleared him.

Unnamed woodchoppers, mostly French Canadians and friends of Resnet; 'a dozen' in the search.

record_check.record: mob threatened to lynch Fred Jackson and pursued him into the woods. He was released from jail and has not been seen since.
record_check.dossier: Sequence is release from Seymour jail, then a barroom beating, then the pursuit; the beating (one Black injured) belongs in the summary.
Eight independent or wire reports in five white papers on the episode itself, plus two reprints and five background items; no Black-press coverage found.

info: Jackson was released on the evening of Wednesday, Feb. 25, 1903, beaten in an Oxford barroom, and hunted through the woods that night; the search continued on the morning of Feb. 26.
Oxford hotel barroom and the woods around Oxford, between Oxford and Derby, Conn.
Fred Jackson, described as 'a negro' of Ansonia (A1) and as 'a farmhand' (A11); Resnet's companion in the hut.

Suspected of murdering Henry Resnet (also called La France), a French Canadian woodchopper whose burned body, with a knife gash, was found in the ruins of his hut; held at Seymour and released by Coroner Mix for insufficient evidence.
A gang of woodchoppers, most of them French Canadians and friends of the dead man; none named.
